topic.title: Minerals, active transport and eutrophication
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Two closely linked outcomes that between them have carried a question in every recent series, and twice a six-mark QWC. The root hair cell arrives on both tiers as a naming and adaptation question [1]-[3]; active transport is Higher and worth [4]; eutrophication is Higher and arrives either as stages to put in order [5]-[6] or as a river or lake survey with a percentage calculation and an explanation of the oxygen fall. Summer 2024's eutrophication question was described by the examiners as strongly discriminating.
mustMemorise: Root hair cell: an EXTENSION giving a large surface area (never describe it as a hair on a head)
Mineral ions in by ACTIVE TRANSPORT; water in by OSMOSIS
Active transport: against the concentration gradient, low to high, requires energy, energy from respiration
Nitrates are absorbed to make amino acids and proteins
Eutrophication: nitrate in → algae bloom → shading and nitrate depletion → plants and algae die → aerobic bacteria decompose and multiply → dissolved oxygen used up → fish and invertebrates die
Name the ION: nitrate or phosphate, never 'nutrients'
It is the DECOMPOSING BACTERIA, not the living algae, that use up the oxygen
notOnThisSpec: Magnesium and chlorophyll — CCEA's B1 names only nitrates, for proteins
Carrier proteins, protein pumps and ATP as the mechanism of active transport
Water potential as a term (osmosis is described in terms of concentration)
Sewage-treatment processes and biological oxygen demand (BOD)

sheet.howExamined: B1 Foundation (60 marks, 1 hour) for the root hair cell's name and adaptation, and B1 Higher (70 marks, 1 hour) for active transport and the whole of eutrophication; calculator allowed. Outcome 1.7.11's third bullet and the whole of 1.7.12 are printed in bold and so are Higher only. Both outcomes have supplied a six-mark QWC in recent series. Schemes are point-for-point and strict: 'against the concentration gradient', 'energy from respiration', and the named ion.

steps.decision: Name the process first. Summer 2024's examiners said only the better answers linked mineral absorption to active uptake at all.

steps.working: They move against the concentration gradient — from the low concentration in the soil water to the higher concentration inside the cell.
steps.decision: State the direction in both forms: the phrase 'against the concentration gradient' and the low-to-high description. Summer 2025's report names the gradient as where most errors were.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Nitrate ions are taken up by active transport. They are moved against the concentration gradient, from the lower concentration in the soil water into the higher concentration inside the cell. This requires energy, and that energy is released by respiration in the root hair cell.

steps.working: The slurry adds nitrates (and phosphates) to the lake water.
steps.decision: Name the ion. Summer 2024's report says answers giving 'nutrients' earned nothing for this point.

steps.working: The nitrate makes the algae and water plants grow and reproduce rapidly, forming an algal bloom.
steps.decision: Say what the nitrate does, not just that it is there.

steps.working: The bloom shades the plants below it, and the nitrate is used up, so the plants and algae die.
steps.decision: Two causes, one consequence. Shading and nitrate depletion are both in the specification's own bullet.

steps.working: Aerobic decomposing bacteria feed on the dead material and multiply, respiring as they do so.
steps.decision: This is the first of the three stages the Summer 2025 report found blank. Name the bacteria as aerobic.

steps.working: Their respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen, so the fish cannot respire and they die.
steps.decision: Finish on oxygen and then on the fish. An answer that stops at 'the bacteria decompose them' loses the two marks the question was really set for.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The slurry adds nitrates to the lake. The extra nitrate makes the algae and water plants grow and reproduce rapidly, forming a bloom at the surface. The bloom shades the plants beneath it and the nitrate is soon used up, so the plants and algae die. Aerobic decomposing bacteria feed on the dead material and multiply, and their aerobic respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen in the water. With too little dissolved oxygen the fish cannot respire, and they die.

twin.stem: Untreated sewage is released into a slow-moving river. Explain why the number of invertebrate species falls just downstream of the outflow.

accepted: the sewage adds nitrate so algae grow rapidly, the bloom shades the plants and the nitrate runs out so they die, aerobic bacteria decompose them and multiply, their respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen and the invertebrates cannot respire so fewer species survive

steps.working: As the oxygen concentration increases the nitrate uptake increases, from 0.4 units at zero oxygen to 7 units.
steps.decision: Describe with numbers taken off the graph. A trend quoted without values is the commonest way to lose the description mark.

steps.working: Above about 8 units of oxygen the uptake levels off and stays at its maximum.
steps.decision: The second half of the description. The plateau is always worth its own mark.

steps.working: Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration, which releases energy.
steps.decision: Now explain. Oxygen is not part of the nitrate ion, so its only possible role is supplying energy.

steps.working: Nitrate must therefore be absorbed by active transport, which needs that energy; with no oxygen there is almost no uptake.
steps.decision: Name the process and use the zero-oxygen reading as the evidence. Diffusion would not depend on oxygen at all.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: As the oxygen concentration increases, nitrate uptake increases sharply, from 0.4 units with no oxygen up to 7 units, after which it levels off at its maximum. Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration, which releases energy, so this shows that nitrate is absorbed by active transport rather than by diffusion: with no oxygen there is almost no energy and almost no uptake.

twin.stem: Suggest why a barley plant growing in a waterlogged field takes up very little nitrate, even when the soil is rich in it.

accepted: a waterlogged soil has no air spaces so there is very little oxygen, the roots cannot respire aerobically and release enough energy, and active transport of nitrate therefore almost stops

items.stem: How does a root hair cell take in mineral ions?

options.text: by active transport
options.feedback: Active transport (active uptake). Summer 2024 examiners said only the better answers made this link.

options.text: by osmosis
options.feedback: Osmosis is how water enters. Mineral ions need active transport.

options.text: by diffusion down the gradient
options.feedback: Diffusion would move ions out of the cell, because the concentration inside is higher.

options.text: by photosynthesis
options.feedback: Photosynthesis makes glucose; it does not move ions. Nitrate is what proteins are made from.

options.text: from a low concentration to a high concentration
options.feedback: Against the gradient — uphill, which is why it costs energy.

options.text: from a high concentration to a low concentration
options.feedback: That is diffusion, and it is free. Summer 2025 examiners reported many errors on this direction.

options.text: in whichever direction the water is moving
options.feedback: Ions and water move independently, and by different processes.

options.text: only when the concentrations are equal
options.feedback: Active transport works precisely when the concentrations are unequal, and it works against the difference.

items.stem: How does water enter a root hair cell?

options.text: by osmosis, needing no energy
options.feedback: Osmosis, down the water's own gradient, with no energy needed.

options.text: by active transport, using energy from respiration
options.feedback: Examiners have reported this in two separate series. Only the mineral ions use active transport.

options.text: by diffusion of water molecules through the cell wall only
options.feedback: The movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane has its own name: osmosis.

options.text: it is pulled in by the nitrate ions
options.feedback: The ions do change the water potential, but the process that moves the water is still osmosis.

items.stem: Which feature identifies a root hair cell in a drawing?

options.text: a long narrow extension from one side
options.feedback: The extension. Summer 2025's mark scheme wanted exactly 'it has no extension' for the cell that was not one.

options.text: it looks like a hair on a person's head
options.feedback: Summer 2025 examiners stated that descriptions in terms of body parts were not accepted.

options.text: it contains chloroplasts
options.feedback: Root hair cells have no chloroplasts — they are underground, with no light.

options.text: it has no nucleus
options.feedback: It has a nucleus like almost every plant cell. What makes it special is its shape.

items.stem: What do plants use absorbed nitrate for?

options.text: to make amino acids and proteins
options.feedback: Proteins, built from amino acids. That is what the specification's bullet says: absorption of nitrates for proteins.

options.text: to make chlorophyll
options.feedback: Chlorophyll is what magnesium is for in other specifications — and magnesium is not on CCEA's B1 at all. Nitrate is for protein.

options.text: as a source of energy
options.feedback: Energy comes from glucose by respiration. Nitrate supplies nitrogen atoms.

options.text: to make starch for storage
options.feedback: Starch is made from glucose and contains no nitrogen.

items.stem: In eutrophication, what uses up the dissolved oxygen?
items.skill: The decomposers, after the algae die

options.text: aerobic bacteria respiring as they decompose the dead plants and algae
options.feedback: The decomposers. Summer 2025 examiners reported the last three stages as the ones left wrong or blank.

options.text: the living algae, as they grow
options.feedback: Living algae photosynthesise and add oxygen to the water. The crisis comes after they die.

options.text: the mat of algae stops oxygen dissolving from the air
options.feedback: A surface mat does reduce the exchange a little, but the marking point is the bacteria respiring.

options.text: the nitrate reacts with the oxygen in the water
options.feedback: No chemical reaction is involved. Living organisms take the oxygen out by respiring.

items.stem: A question asks what is washed off a field into a river to start eutrophication. Which answer scores?

options.text: nitrate from fertiliser
options.feedback: The ion, named. Phosphate is also accepted, and so is the source: fertiliser, slurry or sewage.

options.text: nutrients
options.feedback: Summer 2024 examiners reported that 'nutrients' instead of nitrate or phosphate earned nothing for that point.

options.text: minerals
options.feedback: Too vague in the same way. Which mineral? The mark is for naming it.

options.text: chemicals
options.feedback: Everything is a chemical. Write nitrate or phosphate.

accepted: oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration, which releases energy, so the fact that uptake depends on oxygen shows that nitrate is absorbed by active transport rather than by diffusion

respiration releases the energy
so nitrate must be absorbed by active transport, which needs energy — diffusion would not depend on oxygen

parts.stem: Put the stages of eutrophication into the order in which they happen.

items: Fertiliser, slurry or untreated sewage is washed off the land into the water, adding nitrates (and phosphates).
The extra nitrate makes algae and water plants grow and reproduce rapidly — an algal bloom.
The bloom at the surface shades the plants below, and the nitrate is used up.
Shaded and short of nitrate, the plants and algae die.
Aerobic decomposing bacteria feed on the dead material and multiply.
Those bacteria respire aerobically, so they use up the dissolved oxygen in the water.
With little dissolved oxygen left, fish and aquatic invertebrates cannot respire, and they die.

scheme.for: nitrate from fertiliser or sewage enters the water first
algae and water plants grow rapidly
shading and nitrate depletion
the plants and algae die
aerobic decomposing bacteria feed on them and multiply
the bacteria's respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen, so fish and invertebrates die
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 B1 H Q8: the last three stages proved the most difficult to complete.

hints: Nothing can die before it has grown.
The oxygen only runs out after the decomposers arrive.
parts.workedSolution: 1 Fertiliser, slurry or untreated sewage is washed off the land into the water, adding nitrates (and phosphates). 2 The extra nitrate makes algae and water plants grow and reproduce rapidly — an algal bloom. 3 The bloom at the surface shades the plants below, and the nitrate is used up. 4 Shaded and short of nitrate, the plants and algae die. 5 Aerobic decomposing bacteria feed on the dead material and multiply. 6 Those bacteria respire aerobically, so they use up the dissolved oxygen in the water. 7 With little dissolved oxygen left, fish and aquatic invertebrates cannot respire, and they die.

parts.stem: Describe what happens to the dissolved oxygen along the river from site A to site E.

accepted: the dissolved oxygen falls from 9.6 mg per litre at site A to 3.2 at site C, then rises again to 9.1 at site E

scheme.for: falls from 9.6 mg per litre at A to a lowest value of 3.2 at C
then rises again to 9.1 by site E

hints: Two marks means two parts to the shape.
Quote at least the lowest value.
parts.workedSolution: The dissolved oxygen falls from 9.6 mg per litre at site A to its lowest value of 3.2 mg per litre at site C, just below the outflow, and then rises again as the river flows on, reaching 9.1 mg per litre at site E.

commonErrors.feedback: A description of data needs the data. Quote at least the highest and the lowest readings.

parts.stem:
Calculate the percentage decrease in dissolved oxygen between site A and site C.
Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: Divide by the reading at site A.
parts.workedSolution: Decrease = 9.6 − 3.2 = 6.4 mg per litre. Percentage decrease = 6.4 ÷ 9.6 × 100 = 66.7%.

commonErrors.feedback: Divided by the site C reading. A percentage decrease can never exceed 100%, so 200% shows the denominator is wrong.

parts.stem:
The number of invertebrate species falls from 28 at site A to 6 at site C.
Explain this fall, using the dissolved oxygen readings.

accepted: the dissolved oxygen at site C is much lower because aerobic bacteria decomposing the dead algae have used it up, and invertebrates need dissolved oxygen to respire, so the species that cannot survive the low oxygen die out

scheme.for: aerobic decomposing bacteria have multiplied on the dead algae and plants
their respiration has used up the dissolved oxygen, which is only 3.2 mg per litre at site C
invertebrates need dissolved oxygen to respire, so most species cannot survive and die out

hints: Start with what is consuming the oxygen.
Then say why an animal cannot manage without it.
parts.workedSolution: At site C the dissolved oxygen has fallen to 3.2 mg per litre. Aerobic decomposing bacteria have multiplied on the dead algae and water plants, and their aerobic respiration takes dissolved oxygen out of the water. Aquatic invertebrates need that dissolved oxygen for their own respiration, so most of the species present upstream cannot survive at site C and the number falls from 28 to 6.

commonErrors.feedback: Living algae photosynthesise and add oxygen. It is the aerobic bacteria decomposing them after they die that use the oxygen up.

parts.stem: Suggest why the oxygen and the number of species have both recovered by site E.

accepted: by site E the dead material has been fully decomposed so there are fewer bacteria using oxygen, and oxygen has dissolved back into the water from the air as the river flows

scheme.for: the dead material has been used up, so the bacteria have fallen in number and use less oxygen
oxygen dissolves back into the water from the air as the river flows, so the invertebrates can return

hints: What has happened to the bacteria's food supply four kilometres downstream?
parts.workedSolution: By site E the bacteria have used up the dead algae and plants, so their numbers have fallen and much less oxygen is being taken out of the water. At the same time oxygen dissolves back in from the air as the river flows and mixes, so the dissolved oxygen recovers and invertebrate species can live there again.

parts.stem: Explain why the water plants growing on the bed of the pond die once an algal bloom forms at the surface.

accepted: the bloom at the surface shades the plants below so they cannot get enough light to photosynthesise, and the nitrate has also been used up by the algae

scheme.for: the algal bloom at the surface shades the plants below
so they cannot photosynthesise enough, and the nitrate has also been used up (nitrate depletion)

hints: The specification's bullet names two causes.
parts.workedSolution: The algal bloom forms a dense layer at the surface, which shades the plants growing on the bed so that too little light reaches them to photosynthesise. The rapid growth has also used up the nitrate in the water, so both light and nitrate run short, and the plants die.

commonErrors.feedback: The plants below are short of light, not of oxygen. Shading and nitrate depletion are the two causes the specification names.

parts.stem: Explain, step by step, why there is less oxygen in the pond after the plants and algae have died.

accepted: the dead plants and algae are food for aerobic decomposing bacteria, which multiply rapidly, and because they respire aerobically they take dissolved oxygen out of the water faster than it can be replaced

scheme.for: the dead material is food for aerobic decomposing bacteria
the bacteria multiply rapidly
they respire aerobically, using up the dissolved oxygen in the water

hints: Three links: food, numbers, respiration.
Say what the bacteria do with the oxygen.
parts.workedSolution: The dead plants and algae are a large supply of food for aerobic decomposing bacteria. The bacteria multiply rapidly on it. Because they respire aerobically, every one of them takes dissolved oxygen out of the water, and with so many of them the oxygen is used up faster than it can dissolve back in.

commonErrors.feedback: It is the bacteria, not the algae, that use the oxygen — and only after the algae have died.

parts.stem: Explain why the fish in the pond die.

accepted: fish need dissolved oxygen to respire, and with the bacteria having used it up there is not enough left for them so they suffocate

scheme.for: the dissolved oxygen in the water has fallen too low
fish need dissolved oxygen for respiration, so they cannot respire and die

hints: Say what fish need the oxygen for.
parts.workedSolution: The dissolved oxygen in the water has fallen too low. Fish take dissolved oxygen from the water across their gills and need it for aerobic respiration, so when there is too little left they cannot respire and they die.

context.setting: A farm advised to change how it spreads slurry

parts.stem: Suggest two things a farmer could do to reduce the risk of causing eutrophication in a nearby river.

accepted: spread less fertiliser than the crop can absorb, and leave an unfertilised strip of land between the field and the river

scheme.for: any two from: apply no more fertiliser than the crop can absorb / do not spread before heavy rain / leave an unfertilised strip between the field and the river / store slurry in a sealed tank and spread it in the growing season / treat sewage before releasing it — [1] each

hints: Think about how much, and about when and where.
parts.workedSolution: Apply no more fertiliser than the crop can absorb, so none is left in the soil to be washed away; and leave an unfertilised strip of land between the field and the river so run-off is caught before it reaches the water. (Not spreading slurry just before heavy rain also works.)

parts.stem: Suggest why eutrophication is more likely after a period of heavy rain.

accepted: heavy rain washes more of the nitrate off the fields and into the river, so a much larger amount reaches the water at once

scheme.for: heavy rain washes fertiliser or slurry off the land (run-off)
so more nitrate reaches the river at once and the algae grow faster

hints: What does the rain physically do to nitrate lying in the soil?
parts.workedSolution: Heavy rain runs off the surface of the fields and carries dissolved nitrate with it, so a much larger amount of nitrate reaches the river at once than would otherwise leach slowly through the soil. That sudden supply is what triggers the rapid algal growth.

indicativeContent.point: nitrate from fertiliser (or slurry or sewage) is washed off the land into the lake
the nitrate makes the algae and water plants grow and reproduce rapidly, forming a bloom
the bloom at the surface shades the plants below

parts.workedSolution: Nitrate from the fertiliser spread on the farm was washed off the land into the lake. The extra nitrate made the algae and water plants grow and reproduce rapidly, forming a bloom that turned the water green. The bloom at the surface shaded the plants below it, and the nitrate was soon used up, so the algae and plants died. Aerobic decomposing bacteria fed on all that dead material and multiplied rapidly. Because they respire aerobically they used up the dissolved oxygen in the water. Fish need dissolved oxygen for their own respiration, so with too little left they could not respire and they died. The whole sequence is called eutrophication.

parts.stem:

Describe the structure of this cell, what it takes in, and how each substance enters.

indicativeContent.point: the cell has a long narrow extension reaching out between the soil particles
the extension gives a large surface area for absorption
it has a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and a vacuole, but no chloroplasts
it takes in water from the soil
water enters by osmosis, down its own gradient, needing no energy
it takes in mineral ions such as nitrate
mineral ions enter by active transport, against the concentration gradient
active transport requires energy, which is released by respiration

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Two substances, two processes, and they must not be swapped.
Say 'against the concentration gradient' in full.
parts.workedSolution: The root hair cell has a long, narrow extension that reaches out between the soil particles, and that extension gives it a large surface area for absorption. Like other plant cells it has a cell wall, a cell membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus and a vacuole, but it has no chloroplasts because it is underground. It takes in water from the soil water, and water enters by osmosis, moving down its own gradient through the selectively permeable membrane and needing no energy. It also takes in mineral ions such as nitrate, which are needed to make proteins. Mineral ions enter by active transport, moving against the concentration gradient from the low concentration in the soil to the higher concentration inside the cell. Active transport requires energy, and that energy is released by respiration in the cell's mitochondria.

commonErrors.feedback: Water enters by osmosis. Examiners have reported this exact claim in two separate series, and it costs two of the eight indicative points.
Mineral ions move against the gradient, from low to high. Moving down a gradient is diffusion and needs no energy.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife is asked: 'Describe how a root hair cell takes in water and mineral ions. [4]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: The root hair cell has a long extension which reaches into the soil.
It takes in water and mineral ions by active transport.
They move against the concentration gradient into the cell.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: **Water does not enter by active transport** — it enters by **osmosis**, and osmosis needs no energy. Active transport is the right answer for the mineral ions in the next line, but never for the water.
correction: The root hair cell has a long narrow extension, which gives it a large surface area.
Water enters by osmosis, which needs no energy.
Mineral ions enter by active transport, against the concentration gradient, from the low concentration in the soil to the higher concentration in the cell.
Active transport requires energy, released by respiration.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three marks from four, and the one that got away is the commonest slip in this topic. Build the answer as two columns in your head before you write: **water — osmosis — no energy**, and **mineral ions — active transport — against the gradient — energy from respiration**. Describe the shape as an **extension** too, never as a hair: Summer 2025's mark scheme does not accept body-part comparisons.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niall is asked: 'Explain how fertiliser run-off can kill the fish in a lake. [5]'
His answer:
studentWorking: Nitrate from the fertiliser is washed into the lake.
This makes the algae grow really fast and cover the surface.
The algae use up all the oxygen in the water.
So the fish cannot breathe and they die.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: **The living algae do not use up the oxygen** — while they are alive they photosynthesise and add it. The oxygen falls only **after** the algae die: **aerobic decomposing bacteria** multiply on the dead material and **their** respiration strips the dissolved oxygen out. Two whole stages are missing with it: the **shading and nitrate depletion**, and the **death of the plants and algae**.
correction: Nitrate from the fertiliser is washed into the lake.
The nitrate makes the algae grow and reproduce rapidly, forming a bloom at the surface.
The bloom shades the plants below and the nitrate is used up, so the algae and plants die.
Aerobic decomposing bacteria feed on the dead material, multiply, and use up the dissolved oxygen as they respire.
The fish cannot respire without dissolved oxygen, so they die.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three marks from five. The shape of the story is right and the ion is named, which is the encouraging part; what is missing is the middle of the chain. Count the stages on your fingers as you write: there are **seven**, and the three that examiners report as missing are the middle three — the bloom shading the plants and using up the nitrate, the plants and algae dying, and the bacteria multiplying on the dead material. Keep writing **nitrate** rather than 'nutrients' as well: Summer 2024's examiners wanted the ion named.

prompts.prompt: What adapts a root hair cell for absorption, and what is CCEA's word for that feature?
prompts.answer: It has an extension — a long narrow projection — which gives it a large surface area. Describe it as an extension, not as a hair like one on your head.

prompts.prompt: Give the four things you must say about active transport.
prompts.answer: It moves mineral ions; against the concentration gradient, from low to high; it requires energy; and the energy comes from respiration.

prompts.prompt: How does water enter a root hair cell, and does it need energy?
prompts.answer: By osmosis, down its own gradient. It needs no energy at all. Saying water enters by active transport is an error examiners have reported in two series.

prompts.prompt: Which mineral do plants absorb to make proteins?
prompts.answer: Nitrate. (Magnesium is not on this specification.)

prompts.prompt: Why does nitrate uptake almost stop when there is no oxygen around a root?
prompts.answer: Active transport needs energy, and that energy comes from aerobic respiration. With no oxygen there is no aerobic respiration, so little energy and almost no uptake.

prompts.prompt: Give the seven stages of eutrophication in order.
prompts.answer: 1 fertiliser or sewage washed in; 2 algae and plants grow rapidly; 3 shading, and nitrate runs out; 4 plants and algae die; 5 aerobic bacteria decompose them; 6 oxygen used up; 7 fish and invertebrates die

prompts.prompt: What actually uses up the oxygen in eutrophication?
prompts.answer: Aerobic decomposing bacteria, respiring as they feed on the dead algae and plants. Living algae photosynthesise and add oxygen.

prompts.prompt: Why does 'nutrients are washed into the river' score nothing?
prompts.answer: The mark is for naming the ion: nitrate (or phosphate). Summer 2024 examiners reported that 'nutrients' earned nothing for that point.

prompts.prompt: Why do the water plants on a lake bed die during eutrophication?
prompts.answer: The algal bloom at the surface shades them so they cannot photosynthesise, and the nitrate has been used up.

prompts.prompt: Why do fish die at the end of the eutrophication sequence?
prompts.answer: There is too little dissolved oxygen left in the water for them to respire.
